newsitem.title: JAPAN: World 3rd biggest stock option mkt starts in Japan.
newsitem.headline: World 3rd biggest stock option mkt starts in Japan.

text.p: The world's third-largest stock option market started trade on Friday amid some hesitance, but market participants said more time was needed to measure its chances for long-term success.

"It was much better than we expected," Leigh Baxandall, head of derivatives research at BZW Securities, said of the options which started on the day before a three-day weekend so glitches could be worked out before the next session.
"All 33 stocks have been traded, which has not been the case in the past when new instruments have been introduced," Baxandall added.
Both the Tokyo and Osaka exchanges listed 20 issues each on Friday, a selection which includes blue chips and banks. With seven stocks overlapping, a total 33 stocks were listed.

Brokers said although trade was quiet in general, options on shares such as Sony Corp, whose share price jumped to a record high of 10,900 yen during the session, game maker Nintendo Co Ltd and Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) were fairly popular.
"If liquidity is high for the cash stock, option trading should follow," a trader at a foreign securities house said. "Options trading needs time to grow."
Options are used to hedge against losses due to price fluctuations, allowing investors to buy or sell a specified amount of shares at an agreed price during a set time period.

The individual options started Friday are European-style with five strike prices for each expiry -- an at-the-money strike, two strike levels above and two below. There are only four contract maturities with the most distant, eight months out. The launch will make Japan the largest in market capital following the United States and United Kingdom.
The history of stock derivatives in Japan goes back to the late 1980s, when index futures and options were started.

But a cautious approach has been taken on derivatives on individual stocks, and the lucrative business was banished offshore to less regulated markets, where brokers are able to trade options or warrants on Japanese stocks.

"There are still questions about the liquidity of the market, sidelining institutional investors, and salesmen who do business with private investors still don't have a firm grasp of options," a derivatives trader at a U.S. brokerage said. "Trade today was done mostly by dealers."

But it turned out that even market gurus were a bit muddled about stock options, sending the at-the-money call of Rohm Co Ltd at one point to 500 yen while the put was at the daily limit low of 50 yen.

Despite the hesitant start and the potential opportunities for hedging and earning premiums which options offer, there are still many problems which need to be sorted out before trade takes off, market sources said.

The Japan Securities Dealers' Association has yet to decide how taxes will be assessed when margin transactions are used at the time of settlement. A decision is due by mid-September, when the first contract matures.

"The most active centre for derivatives is the United States, much of that has been driven by the ability to get retail investors involved in the market," BZW's Baxandall said. "It involves a strong education process."
